title: Evolution Strategies Beat GRPO on Reasoning Coverage
hook: GRPO sharpens one answer and collapses entropy. Evolution strategies keep the population diverse — improving pass@1 while also raising pass@k, which GRPO gives up.
key_points: Evolution Strategies (ES) had been treated as a memory-efficient but weaker alternative to GRPO for reasoning post-training.
The paper shows ES yields broader reasoning coverage, better exploiting what the pretrained model already knows.
Theory: verifier-projected Jensen-Shannon diversity across the ES population helps pass@K.
Empirically ES improves pass@1 while attaining higher pass@K, whereas GRPO shows entropy collapse.
A sequential GRPO-then-ES recipe combines GRPO's pass@1 strength with ES's pass@K gains.
Gains come from a sparse subset of large-magnitude updates despite huge whole-model parameter drift — and without catastrophic forgetting.
content_html: Evolution Strategies — perturb the weights, keep what scores better, no backprop through the reward — reappeared recently as a memory-cheap way to post-train LLMs for reasoning. The assumption was that you pay for the memory saving in quality. Ba and colleagues argue the trade is not what people thought.
extra_html:
The finding

ES gives broader reasoning coverage than GRPO. Theoretically, the authors tie pass@K to verifier-projected Jensen-Shannon diversity across the ES population: a spread-out population explores more distinct solution paths. Empirically, GRPO exhibits the familiar entropy collapse — the policy narrows, pass@1 goes up, pass@K stalls or drops — while ES improves pass@1 and attains higher pass@K. Since pass@K is the honest measure of what a model can find when allowed multiple attempts, that matters for anything with a verifier in the loop.

Two secondary results are interesting on their own. Sequential GRPO-then-ES gets both properties. And although ES drifts a large fraction of the model's parameters, the task gains are carried by a sparse subset of larger-magnitude updates — held-out evaluations show no catastrophic forgetting. Big parameter movement, it turns out, need not mean big functional change.

Why it matters

It repositions ES as a distinct post-training paradigm with its own advantage scope, rather than a budget substitute for policy-gradient RL. The authors also note a practical scaling quirk: larger models need smaller ES populations.

related.title: GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization
related.hook: GRPO dropped the value network from PPO and scored each answer against a group of sampled siblings — the cheap RL recipe that made DeepSeek-R1's reasoning trainable.

related.title: Use a Weak Model to Stop Your Strong One Getting Stuck
related.hook: RLVR collapses a model's entropy until it only knows one way to think. Feeding it half-finished reasoning from a smaller, worse model breaks the rut — no reward engineering required.

flashcards.prompt: What is entropy collapse, and why does it hurt pass@k?
flashcards.back_html: The policy's output distribution narrows during RL training. Pass@1 can improve, but the model stops producing varied attempts, so drawing k samples no longer explores k different reasoning paths.

flashcards.prompt: What does the paper report about where ES's performance gains come from?

choices.text: A sparse subset of large-magnitude updates, despite drift across most parameters
Uniform small updates spread evenly across all layers
Changes confined entirely to the final output projection

flashcards.explanation_html: Whole-model parameter drift is substantial, but task gains trace to a small set of larger updates — large parameter movement does not imply widespread functional change.

flashcards.prompt: How do the authors propose combining ES and GRPO?
flashcards.back_html: Sequentially: train with GRPO for its pass@1 strength, then with ES to recover the reasoning coverage that raises pass@K.
